questions.title_en: How much must one do to fulfill the mitzvah of bikur cholim?
questions.question:
In Ahavas Chesed Chelek Gimmel Perek Beis, the Chofetz Chaim discusses the Mitzvah of Bikur Cholim and how people בעוונותינו הרבים העולם מקלין במצוה זו.

He also writes there that:

מצות ביקור חולים אין לו שעור ... אפילו כמה פעמים ביום

What is the גדר for how many visits one should make to the sick person?

The Chofetz Chaim talks about multiple times per day, does that mean one must do so at least once a day? What if the person is an hour drive away, how much effort or how often must the visit.

Is there any distance at which someone doesn't have to make an effort to visit the sick person?

answers.text:
The Kitzur Shulchan Aruch in סימן קצג - הלכות בקור חולים highlights the main purpose of Bikur Cholim. Dropping in & out for a few seconds is not the idea.

The main purposes are:

  • כַּמָּה פְעָמִים בַּיוֹם. וְכָל הַמּוֹסִיף, הֲרֵי זֶה מְשֻׁבָּח, וּבִלְבַד שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה לָטֹרַח עַל הַחוֹלֶה.‏

As you mentioned, go often if possible, but ensure you're not being a burden on the patient. (I would add: or their caretakers.)

Going too often to the point that they have to entertain you, is counterproductive. Being there when the Doctors make their rounds or a favorite friend or family member is there is not a great idea.

  • עִקַּר מִצְוַת בִּקּוּר חוֹלִים הוּא לְעַיֵן בְּצָרְכֵי הַחוֹלֶה מַה הוּא צָרִיךְ לַעֲשׂוֹת לוֹ, וְשֶׁיִמְצָא נַחַת רוּחַ עִם חֲבֵרָיו, וְגַם שֶׁיִתֵּן דַעְתּוֹ עָלָיו וִיבַקֵּשׁ רַחֲמִים עָלָיו. וְאִם בִּקֵּר וְלֹא בִקֵּשׁ, לֹא קִיֵם אֶת הַמִּצְוָה.‏

The main purpose of your visit should be to see how you can be of assistance. Maybe a caretaker needs a ride, or a bill to be paid or some shopping or food. Possibly bring something to read for the patient or the caretakers.

It should be a pleasant visit; make sure the patient is enjoying themselves because you're there. Keep the mood light, or learn with them if that's what they want. Or sing or discuss sports - but make sure the patient is enjoying it, not just smiling to make the visitor feel good. Maybe prepare a fun story or some good news.

Don't forget to pray for the patient. In their presence it can be in any language and you don't need their full name. "Please Hashem let my buddy lying here have a swift & full recovery". Not davening defeats the purpose

  • הַמְבַקְּרִים יְדַבְּרוּ אִתּוֹ בְּהַשְׂכֵּל וָדַעַת, וְיֹאמְרוּ לוֹ, דְבָרִים מְחַיִּים, וְלֹא דְבָרִים מְמִיתִים. וְיֹאמְרוּ לוֹ, שֶׁיִתֵּן דַּעְתּוֹ עַל עִנְיָנָיו, אִם הִלְוָה אוֹ הִפְקִיד אֵצֶל אֲחֵרִים אוֹ אֲחֵרִים אֶצְלוֹ, וְאַל יְפַחֵד מִפְּנֵי זֶה מֵהַמָּוֶת.‏

The mood should be positive and upbeat; not morbid. That said, for terminally ill patients it may be appropriate to discuss his will and last testament, debts and POAs. But only if you are the right person in the right place.

You are supposed to be of assistance and not trying to dig into their private affairs.

Discussing how death is a rebirth into a better world is appropriate, if you're well-versed in the subject matter and can do it nicely.

So there's no fixed rules for how often to go. But if going daily means the patient feels bad that you're spending most of your free time visiting them, then maybe you're going too often.

As long as you're being helpful, and the patient is thrilled to see you, you're doing it right.

questions.title_en: Jewish Holidays and Susceptibility to Tuma due to contact with liquids
questions.question:
What is a connection between Yamim Tovim an the 7 liquids that render food susseptible to tumah? Here's the background of the question. Elsewhere the connection was presented (as written below) but not explained.

Mishna Makhshirin 6:4 lists 7 liquids which enable fruits and produce be susceptible to tuma upon a contact:

שִׁבְעָה מַשְׁקִין הֵן. הַטַּל וְהַמַּיִם, הַיַּיִן וְהַשֶּׁמֶן, וְהַדָּם, וְהֶחָלָב, וּדְבַשׁ דְּבוֹרִים. דְּבַשׁ צְרָעִים, טָהוֹר, וּמֻתָּר בַּאֲכִילָה:

There are seven liquids: dew, water, wine, oil, blood, milk and bees’ honey. Hornets’ honey does not cause susceptibility to uncleanness and may be eaten.

The curious fact is that each liquid is used during Jewish holidays:

  1. On Rosh Hashanah we dip apple in bees' honey.
  2. On Succot water is poured on the altar in the Temple and the world is judged for water.
  3. On Shemini Atzert we pray for rain, which is water from shamayim, i.e. dew
  4. On Chanukkah we burn oil on the menorah
  5. On Purim we drink wine
  6. On Pesach we talk about events in Egypt, such as the blood of korban Pesach and the blood of milla, red wine is used to symbolize the blood of korban Pesach.
  7. On Shavuot we have a dairy meal which has milk products.

Is there a connection? What are the sources?

As pointed out, this connection (perhaps in a slightly different order) has been noted in several places, such as by R' Mordechai Kornfeld https://dafyomi.co.il/parsha/7liquids.htm, but not really explained. The food coming in contact with liquids not only becomes susceptible to tuma, but also it can acquire a loftier status of kedusha as maasrot, teruma, mincha. In what way is it similar to the way Jewish holidays impact Jewish people?

שלום,
השנה סבתי נפטרה וזאת הייתה פעם ראשונה בה השתתפתי בהלוויה. היא גרה ברוסיה ולכן כנראה שהטקס היה פחות שגרתי. לפני שיצאנו לקבורה עצמה הרב שהעביר את הטקס אמר שאפשר לקבל מחילה ולמחול לנפטר פעם אחרונה כדי לישר את ההדורים ולהיפרד בשלום. ולאחר שמבקשים סליחה אומרים תפילה קטנה. אני לא זוכרת בדיוק מה הייתה התפילה... אני חושבת שאמרתי שלוש פעמים  "שרוי ומחול ומותר״ שזה בעצם חלק מהתר ומכל נדרי ביום כיפור. רציתי לשאול אם אתה מכיר את המנהג הזה ותוכל לדייק אותו בשבילי. תודה רבה ושבוע טוב. 
אסתר

שלום וברכה.
תמיד מבקשים מחילה מהנפטר בשעת הקבורה. בדרך כלל כאן בארץ, החברא קדישא שהם אחראים על הקבורה, אומרים נוסח מיוחד של בקשת מחילה בשמם ובשם המשפחה והידידים. כל אחד יכול לבקש מחילה המנפטר באופן כללי או אם יש לו בקשה מסויימת של מחילה. וכך גם ראוי. 
 מו השמים תנוחמו.

questions.title_en: Is there such a thing as 75% lifnei iver?
questions.question:
My question is pretty hypothetical, so I'll try to give an example.

Let's say person A is in a situation where they are committing an aveirah (sin) according to the majority of halachic opinions, yet there is a minority opinion that considers him to not be transgressing.

If person B were to change the situation and render it forbidden according to all halachic opinions, would person B transgress the prohibition of "lifnei iver"? Do we consider him as having caused person A to have conclusively transgressed, or can person B claim that, according to the majority of opinions, person A was already in a state of transgression and therefore, according to most opinions, he hasn't compounded the transgression in any way?

Fundamentally, I am asking if a stricter, more authorative opinion in halacha at least acknowledges the validity of a lenient, less-authorative opinion, in a situation where the lenient opinion leads to a chumra - viz. lifnei iver.

(For an example of this case, consider somebody leaving a premises in a likely case of yichud - whatever the circumstances need to be to fulfil this hypothetical.)

NOTE: this question asks if it is lifnei iver to cause someone to transgress something that is forbidden according to the way they pasken the halacha. My question is something else.

questions.title_he: מִזְבֵּחַ marked with פשטא and accentuated מלרע?
questions.question:
It is my understanding that the absolute noun מִזְבֵּחַ is never marked with just one פשטא (and accentuated מלרע) but always שני פשטין (and accentuated מלעיל), the latter in accordance with its proper stress on the penultimate syllable. For example:

בראשית 12:8

שמות 28:43, 29:37, 30:20, 38:4

ויקרא 1:5, 1:16, 9:7, 16:12

במדבר 4:26, 17:11, 18:3, 18:17

However, I recently came across a fascinating Yemenite חומש in תאג׳ תורה קדומה and all 13 cases have it marked with one פשטא and accentuated מלרע. The "חלק הדקדוק" there to שמות 29:37 (see a more detailed commentary here and especially here) explains as follows:

לז. והיה המזבח֙. בפשטא אחת והיא מלרע, בכל ספרי תימן, והיא שיטת מהרי״ץ בכל מקום. ובתאג י״ם לא עמדו על דעת רבינו בזה ועשאוה בתרין פשטין היפך דעתו והיפך התיגאן, ופשוט. שוב מצאתי גילוי גדול לדעת רבינו במוסרת תאג קדמון בפרשת ויקהל על פס׳ ויעש למזבח מכבר דמסיר עלה ׳למזבח, כלהון ביתיב חד׳ הרי זה בניין אב לכל המקרא שלעולם לא תבוא תיבת המזבח בתרין פשטין אלא בפשט אחד. ומעתה אָבַד סִבְרוֹ וּבָטַל סֵיכוּיוֹ של כל הבא לחלוק על דברי מוסרה זו שקבעוה קמאי דקמאי עפ״י חכמי המוסרה. יפ״ה׃

Do any non-Yemenite commentators/grammarians address the possibility of מִזְבֵּחַ shifting from מלעיל to מלרע and having פשטא to reflect that syntax? (The second link, ד״ה כמובן, notes that the מנחת שי is silent on this matter.)

questions.title_he: דרך Segol or kometz under ד
questions.question:
In Parshas Balak (probably other places too), the word “דרך" is usually vocalized as ״דֶרֶך״; but at least once, it’s vocalized as ״דָרֶך״ with a kometz. Why?

Also, sometimes Bilaam and Balak have a Beis and sometimes a Vais. This change also happens with other names in other parshiyos. Why?

answers.text:
there is derech; "way", or dorech when it is an esnachta or sof passuk

In Balak, there is the word dorach; which means something else.

Your question, as of now, includes two sub-questions. I will answer both.

A) A Segolate is a word that ends with one unstressed Segol, such as חֶסֶד and קֹדֶשׁ.
The most common type of Segolate ends with two Segols in a row. This includes דֶרֶך, לֶחֶם, יֶרֶך, דֶגֶל, מַחְבֶרֶת, and more.
When such a Segolate is at a major break in a פסוק—that is, when it takes an אֶתנַחתָא/אַתנָח or when it’s the last word in a פסוק—the first Segol changes to a Kamatz. Thus, דֶרֶך becomes דָרֶך, and לֶחֶם becomes לָחֶם, and more.

B) There are two types of Dagesh: Dagesh Chazzaq and Dagesh Qal.
Dagesh Chazzaq indicates that a letter is geminated, i.e. that it lasts twice as long and is pronounced with a little extra force. It is not relevant to your question.
Dagesh Qal occurs only on the letters בגדכפ״ת. It gives them their “hard” pronunciation. For example, it turns Vet into Bet.

Dagesh Qal occurs on a letter only if it doesn’t come after a vowel. This is easy to understand within a word, but it’s a bit more complicated when we’re talking about the first letter of a word, like the ב in בלק. For that, the rule is as follows:
If the preceding word 1) ends in a vowel, AND 2) has a conjunctive trope sign, then the first letter of the next word doesn’t get a Dagesh Qal. In every other case, it DOES get a Dagesh Qal.
Thus, for example, in the phrase דִּבְרֵי בָלָק, Balaq’s name is pronounced with a Vet, because the previous word ends in a vowel and has a conjunctive trope.
If it's דָ֫רֶך it means the word is in pause, meaning that the accent is a disjunctive one, so it lengthens it. Sometimes a shva become a qamets or a tsere if it's in pause

questions.title_en: Midrashim that explore the exact meaning of "tov" in Genesis 1?
questions.question:
It's no secret that "good," in English as well as in Hebrew, is rather polysemous: on the one hand, it can mark the degree to which a given thing satisfies its purpose or relevant ideal (as in a "good table," "good car," etc: in each case, the specifications of "good" are relative to the noun that follows it); on the other, it can identify moral righteousness — good in the unqualified, ethical sense.

As such, I'm wondering about the history of the interpretation of the word "good" ("tov") as it appears in Creation, specifically in Genesis 1. My question isn't what the word means, but rather when and how Jewish readers attempted to establish its meaning, using either the exegetical tools of midrash or those of philosophy. That is: when and where, exactly, do we see an attempt to define the Creational "tov" in biblical commentary?

Unsurprisingly, I've found relevant passages in Midrash Lekach Tov, but I'm wondering if this is really the starting point for my search. Is there anything earlier, or indeed, anything else at all? It would seem to be a question with major conceptual stakes, at least for the modern reader...

answers.text:
I would have preferred this to be a comment rather than an answer, but so far, I lack those privileges.

A great source for the discussion of what is tov can be found in the Maharal's commentary to Avot 1:2. On Sefaria

questions.title_en: What is unique about Asaf, the author of some Tehillim?
questions.question: Particularly now in 5784 with the war in Eretz Yisrael and rising open antisemitism across the world, many Rabbonim (e.g. the Agudah, OU, etc.) are suggesting we say Tehillim 79, 80, and 83 among others. Although Asaf did not write many perakim, those three are particularly among the ones he authored - what is unique about Asaf that he merited to have his Tehillim said during particularly difficult times in exile?

שלום כבוד הרב
נתתי את הדולרים לבן שלי.
זו לא היתה הלוואה, אלא מעין פיקדון ע"מ שיחזיר לי אחרי שהחליף לדולרים תקינים, או, שיחזיר לי תמורתם בש"ח לפי שער יציג כשיחזור מחו"ל. אינני זוכר אם אמרתי לו בפרוש את עניין השער היציג כשיחזיר, אבל ברור שזו היתה מחשבתי.
הדולרים הישנים שנתתי לו הם הילך תקין בארה"ב ואין בעיה להשתמש בהם.

שלום וברכה,

ההבדל בין הלוואה לפקדון הוא שבהלוואה הכסף שניתן שייך למקבל, והמקבל צריך להחזיר כסף אחר לאחר זמן. ובפקדון הכסף נשאר בבעלות הנותן.
במקרה שלך לפי הבנתי הכסף שנתת לבנך, לאחר שנתת לו שייך לו, והוא התחייב להחזיר לך תמורתם לאחר זמן, א"כ זו הלוואה.

בארץ ישראל השקל הוא הכסף שבו משתמשים, והדולרים הם פחות שימושיים, לכן הדולרים אינם נחשבים כסף אלא חפצים. לכן כאשר אדם מלווה דולרים יש בעיה לקבל חזרה דולרים כיוון שהשער שלהם משתנה ביחס לשקל ויש אפשרות שהמלווה יקבל חזרה דולר שערכו גדול יותר ממה שהלווה. לכן כאשר מלווים דולר יש להמידו לשקל על פי ערך השקל בזמן ההלוואה. אך ישנה עוד דרך, והיא שאם יש ללווה דולרים (אפילו מעט) ניתן להלוות לו דולרים והלווה יצטרך להחזיר דולרים. ובאופן זה יוכל הלווה לפרוע גם בשקלים לפי ערך הדולר בזמן הפרעון.
לכן אם היה לבן שלך דולרים בזמן ההלוואה אין כאן בעיה של ריבית. ואם לא היה לו, יש בעיה ועליו לפרוע ע"פ השער שהיה בזמן ההלוואה.

בברכה,

שלום כבוד הרב,
רציתי לשאול לגבי לבישת נעליים או לפחות גרביים בעת נטילת ידיים. שמעתי כי יש להקפיד ללבוש לפחות נעלים או גרביים או לברך על השטיח שתהיה מחיצה בין הרגליים לרצפה אחרת זה נראה כמנהג אבלות. 
האם באמת יש צורך להקפיד על כך?
תודה רבה 

אין איסור ללכת יחף, אבל הולך כך כל השבעה, בשונה מאדם רגיל שהולך מידי פעם.
(יש על פי המקובלים לא ללכת יחפים בתשעה באב, , או לשבת על הרצפה בקינות או בתיקון חצות, ובכלל חשיבות לקנות נעליים - בן איש חי - דברים כ, כא. וישלח יא, יח , חכמי הנגלה לא חששו לזה, ובוודאי בברכות מותר)
ברכה והצלחה

questions.title_en: Why were only men allowed to divorce for sexual impurity? Did men not also commit sexual misconduct?
questions.question:
Note: this question was posted to Biblical Hermeneutics yesterday, and did not attract a response. As this is a question about the Law of Moses, I'm open to a Jewish explanation as well. This question seems related, though not the same; but I am looking for a more Bible-focused explanation, as the rest of additional Jewish traditions are unfamiliar to me: Can a wife demand a divorce from a cheating husband.

In Deuteronomy 22 and 24, only men were allowed to produce a bill of divorce. Although in the case of adultery, both sexes are criminally responsible, in the case of Deuteronomy 22 and 24, there does not seem to be an equivalent law for women finding such uncleanness in their husband.

(Deuteronomy 24:1, Koren trans.) When a man has taken a wife, and married her, and it come to pass that she find no favour in his eyes, because he has found some unseemliness in her: then let him write her a bill of divorce, and give it in her hand, and send her out of his house.

(Deuteronomy 22:13-15, Koren trans.) If any man take a wife, and go in to her, and hate her, and lay accusing speeches against her, and bring out an evil name upon her, saying, I took this woman, and when I came to her, I found her not to be a virgin: then shall the father of the girl, and her mother, take and bring forth the tokens of the girl’s virginity to the elders of the city in the gate

It is my understanding that rabbis generally also allowed women to divorce their husbands. That is a broader issue. But the more specific question is, could there not be uncleanness found in a man, as in general sexual indecency, impropriety, or something of the like, which, though not at the level of adultery (for which the punishment is death), would legally allow divorce -- a male equivalent to women's purity laws? And if not, why not?

Obviously the Bible is not completely egalitarian, but I wonder how to address this in today's context, where this is seen as a slight against women, who would not have had the same recourse as men. How do theologians explain this apparent unfairness towards women?

Duplicate note:

The following duplicate has been suggested: In adultery, why is a wife is guilty, and a husband not?. The proposed duplicate asks why the husband is not guilty. My question asks why the wife has no recourse.

Related questions:

Did Moses compromise by allowing the Israelites to divorce in Deutoronomy 24:1?

What does the phrase "uncleanliness in her" refer to in Deuteronomy 24:1?

answers.text:
B"H

First, that reference from Deuteronomy 22:13-15 (really extending to -20 and on) is talking about a case where she cheated on him after becoming engaged to him but before marrying him, which is a capital offense.

Rashi ibid:20

  1. But if this matter was true: [indeed,] no evidence of the girl's virginity was found. כ. וְאִם־אֱמֶ֣ת הָיָ֔ה הַדָּבָ֖ר הַזֶּ֑ה לֹֽא־נִמְצְא֥וּ בְתוּלִ֖ים לַנַּֽעֲרָֽה (כתיב לנער)

But if this matter was true: [as corroborated] by witnesses, and there was warning, [proving] that she had committed adultery after her betrothal. — [Keth. 44b]

וְאִם־אֱמֶת הָיָה הַדָּבָר: בְּעֵדִים וְהַתְרָאָה, שֶׁזִּנְּתָה לְאַחַר אֵרוּסִין (כתובות מ"ד):

According to Torah law, a man is allowed to have more than one wife, but not the other way around. There's no unique "sin" for a man to commit adultery as there is for a woman (besides for the other sins involved for having relations with someone he's not married to/a niddah etc), although if he does cheat on her then that is grounds for her to initiate a divorce (see later).

In terms of being "fair" and "moral": morality is defined by the Creator. He made everything, He decides what's good and what's bad.

The Rambam tells us that all of the laws of forbidden relationships are known as chukim, Mitzvos who's reasoning is not known to us.

They have deep spiritual reasons, some that only the Creator knows about, but not all of them can be understood by the intellect of created beings.

The Rambam does say that however much reason one can give these commandments, one should give (end of h. Meila), but (ibid) the main reason of them is still hidden from us.

In terms of a woman being able to divorce a man because of immodest behavior, many rabbis say that if she simply doesn't want to continue being with him then she can initiate a divorce, especially if the man has been involved excessively with other women, even when no adultery was found.

A woman may demand a divorce from her husband, if he has been found to be philandering with other women. There need not be proof of his having committed adultery, just of his having cavorted with other women. Even his causing her a bad name through his lecherous actions is likewise considered legitimate justification for the wife launching a divorce action. If the wife feels repulsed by her husband, it is wrong to force her to remain in the union

Now to the question of what specifically is meant by "immodest behavior" by the women, the Rambam references the verse in hilchos geirushin 10:20-22:

22 It is a mitzvah to divorce a woman who possesses unsavory character traits and does not conduct herself modestly73, as is the practice of proper daughters of Israel, as [implied by Proverbs 22:10]: "Drive away the scoffer, and contention will depart."

When a woman has been divorced for loose moral conduct,74 it is not fitting for a proper man to marry her, lest people say: "This one sent away this wicked woman, and this one brought her home."

כב אִשָּׁה רָעָה בְּדֵעוֹתֶיהָ וְשֶׁאֵינָהּ צְנוּעָה כִּבְנוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל הַכְּשֵׁרוֹת מִצְוָה לְגָרְשָׁהּ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (משלי כב י) ״‎גָּרֵשׁ לֵץ וְיֵצֵא מָדוֹן״‎. וְאִשָּׁה שֶׁנִּתְגָּרְשָׁה מִשּׁוּם פְּרִיצוּת אֵין רָאוּי לְאָדָם כָּשֵׁר שֶׁיִּשָּׂאֶנָּה. שֶׁלֹּא יֹאמְרוּ זֶה הוֹצִיא רְשָׁעָה מִבֵּיתוֹ וְזֶה מַכְנִיסָהּ:

And in hilchos ishus 24:11-12 the Rambam explains exactly what is meant:

11 The following are the actions for which a woman is considered to have "violated the faith of Moses":

a) going out to the marketplace with her hair uncovered;25

b) taking vows or oaths that she does not keep;

c) engaging in sexual relations [with her husband] while in the niddah state;

d) failing to separate challah or feeding her husband food that is forbidden to eat - needless to say, this applies to forbidden crawling animals and animals that were not ritually slaughtered; it applies even to produce that was not tithed.26

How can the latter [two] matters be known? For example, she said: "So and so, the priest, [separated tithes] from this produce for me," "So and so separated challah [from this dough]," "So and so, the Sage, said this stain does not render me a niddah" - and after eating the food or engaging in sexual relations with her, the husband asked the person whose name was mentioned and he denied the occurrence of the incident. Another example: a woman's [conduct caused] it to be established in her neighborhood that she was in the niddah state,27 but she told her husband that she was ritually pure. He engaged in relations with her [and afterwards discovered the truth].

יא וְאֵלּוּ הֵן הַדְּבָרִים שֶׁאִם עָשְׂתָה אַחַת מֵהֶן עָבְרָה עַל דַּת משֶׁה. יוֹצְאָה בַּשּׁוּק וּשְׂעַר רֹאשָׁהּ גָּלוּי. אוֹ שֶׁנּוֹדֶרֶת אוֹ שֶׁנִּשְׁבַּעַת וְאֵינָהּ מְקַיֶּמֶת. אוֹ שֶׁשִּׁמְּשָׁה מִטָּתָהּ וְהִיא נִדָּה. אוֹ שֶׁאֵינָהּ קוֹצָה לָהּ חַלָּה. אוֹ שֶׁהֶאֱכִילָה אֶת בַּעְלָהּ דְּבָרִים אֲסוּרִים, אֵין צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר שְׁקָצִים וּרְמָשִׂים וּנְבֵלוֹת, אֶלָּא דְּבָרִים שֶׁאֵינָן מְעֻשָּׂרִין. וְהֵיאַךְ יוֹדֵעַ דָּבָר זֶה כְּגוֹן שֶׁאָמְרָה לוֹ פֵּרוֹת אֵלּוּ פְּלוֹנִי כֹּהֵן תִּקְּנָם לִי וְעִסָּה זוֹ פְּלוֹנִית הִפְרִישָׁה לִי חַלָּתָהּ וּפְלוֹנִי הֶחָכָם טִהֵר לִי אֶת הַכֶּתֶם וְאַחַר שֶׁאָכַל אוֹ בָּא עָלֶיהָ שָׁאַל אוֹתוֹ פְּלוֹנִי וְאָמַר לֹא הָיוּ דְּבָרִים מֵעוֹלָם. וְכֵן אִם הֻחְזְקָה נִדָּה בִּשְׁכֵנוֹתֶיהָ וְאָמְרָה לְבַעְלָהּ טְהוֹרָה אֲנִי וּבָא עָלֶיהָ:

12 What is meant by "the Jewish faith"? The customs of modesty that Jewish women practice. When a woman performs any of the following acts, she is considered to have violated the Jewish faith:

a) she goes to the marketplace or a lane with openings at both ends without having her head [fully] covered - i.e., her hair is covered by a handkerchief, but not with a veil like all other women,28

b) she spins [flax or wool] with a rose on her face29 - on her forehead or on her cheek - like immodest gentile women,

c) she spins in the marketplace and shows her forearms to men;30

d) she plays frivolously with young lads,

e) she demands sexual intimacy from her husband in a loud voice until her neighbors hear her talking about their intimate affairs, or

f) she curses her husband's father in her husband's presence.31

יב וְאֵי זוֹ הִיא דָּת יְהוּדִית הוּא מִנְהַג הַצְּנִיעוּת שֶׁנָּהֲגוּ בְּנוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל. וְאֵלּוּ הֵן הַדְּבָרִים שֶׁאִם עָשְׂתָה אַחַת מֵהֶן עָבְרָה עַל דָּת יְהוּדִית. יוֹצְאָה לַשּׁוּק אוֹ לְמָבוֹי מְפֻלָּשׁ וְרֹאשָׁהּ פָּרוּעַ וְאֵין עָלֶיהָ רְדִיד כְּכָל הַנָּשִׁים. אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁשְּׂעָרָהּ מְכֻסֶּה בְּמִטְפַּחַת. אוֹ שֶׁהָיְתָה טוֹוָה בַּשּׁוּק וּוֶרֶד וְכַיּוֹצֵא בּוֹ כְּנֶגֶד פָּנֶיהָ עַל פַּדַּחְתָּהּ אוֹ עַל לְחָיֶיהָ כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁעוֹשׂוֹת הָעַכּוּ''ם הַפְּרוּצוֹת. אוֹ שֶׁטּוֹוָה בַּשּׁוּק וּמַרְאֵית זְרוֹעוֹתֶיהָ לִבְנֵי אָדָם. אוֹ שֶׁהָיְתָה מְשַׂחֶקֶת עִם הַבַּחוּרִים. אוֹ שֶׁהָיְתָה תּוֹבַעַת הַתַּשְׁמִישׁ בְּקוֹל רָם מִבַּעְלָהּ עַד שֶׁשְּׁכֵנוֹתֶיהָ שׁוֹמְעוֹת אוֹתָהּ מְדַבֶּרֶת עַל עִסְקֵי תַּשְׁמִישׁ. אוֹ שֶׁהָיְתָה מְקַלֶּלֶת אֲבִי בַּעְלָהּ בִּפְנֵי בַּעְלָהּ:

The verses you are quoting do not support your thesis that there is only a concept of "sexual decency" for women but not men. See Y DJ's answer for a basic Scriptual source that proves men are not allowed to be indecent, and there are many more.

The Torah is very concerned about marriages. A marriage is a sacred bond between a man and a woman. The Torah recognises that sometimes a marriage has lost certain qualities - including a solid bond between the husband and wife - and therefore it would be better that they are divorced rather than remain married.

The verses you are quoting are not providing any more information than the following:

  1. A husband must initiate a divorce (24)
  2. A husband must do so willingly (24)
  3. A example of grounds for him to do so would be if he finds his wife to be repulsive (24, and the Torah is recognising that most men find sexual indecency in women to be repuslive, as an example)
  4. If a woman tells her husband she is a virgin before marriage, and he discovers that she isn't, that is grounds for divorce (22 - see also Core of reality's answer regarding how this is related to actual adultery, rather than virginity - it is allowed for a Jew to marry a non-virgin)
  5. Her family has the opportunity to prove her innocence, and clear her name (22).
  6. If her innocence is proven, he is punished (22).

These are general principles and they do not imply anything about what a woman can and can't ask for a divorce for, so there is no use making presumptions. Indeed, looking at point 3) we can learn that if a woman finds her husband repulsive, she very likely has the right to demand a divorce, and courts will enforce it.

This can include him being sexually promiscuous, not providing her conjugal rights, not supporting her financially, losing a limb, or even developing bad breath! See SA EH 154.

It is fair to note that the Torah does concern itself with a woman's sexual purity more than a man's, but that is for several reasons that, again, do not imply that there is no such thing as indecency by men. It's partly legal, partly practical, and partly just recognition of basic human psychology - men and women's concerns are asymmetrical, but asymmetry does not imply bias or unfairness.

There is a clear prohibition for promiscuity Devarim 23:18 for both men and women:

לֹא־תִהְיֶ֥ה קְדֵשָׁ֖ה מִבְּנ֣וֹת יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וְלֹֽא־יִהְיֶ֥ה קָדֵ֖שׁ מִבְּנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃

There shall be no Jewish woman promiscuous/prostitute, and not a Jewish man be promiscuous/prostitute.

The understanding of the words קָדֵ֖שׁ / קְדֵשָׁ֖ה may have association with ancient cults like Babylonian Ishtar, but in modern times it seems to be interpreted as promiscuous on the OU website https://outorah.org/p/6168. I do not know if this is strong enough to be grounds for divorce, especially when either a man or a woman can do teshuvah.

questions.title_he: מעשר כספים לבן שלומד חלקית בכולל
questions.question:
שלום רב,
בני הנשוי לומד כעשרים שעות שבועיות בכולל בישיבה, האם כסף שאני נותנת לו כתמיכה כספית יכול להיחשב כמעשר כספים?

שלום וברכה!

באופן עקרוני, תמיכה בבן שלומד בכולל יכולה להיחשב כמעשר כספים (שולחן ערוך יורה דעה רנ"א, ג).
לגבי המצב שאת מתארת, שהוא לומד בכולל באופן חלקי בלבד: אני מניח שבשאר הזמן הוא עובד. אם כך, הדבר תלוי בשאלה האם סך כל ההכנסות של המשפחה (מהעבודה, מילגת הכולל, עבודה של האשה וכדומה) מספיק כדי לכסות את הצרכים הנחוצים שלהם. אם ההכנסות שלהם מספיקות לצרכים הנחוצים, הם לא נחשבים כנזקקים. גם אם הם חיים בצמצום יחסית לאנשים אחרים, ואת תומכת בהם כלכלית כדי שיחיו יותר ברווח, העזרה הזו אינה נחשבת כמעשר כספים. אם הם לא מצליחים לכסות את הצרכים הנחוצים, הם נחשבים כנזקקים והתמיכה בהם נחשבת כמעשר כספים.

questions.title_en: How do Jews who believe in evolution explain kosher species and kilayim?
questions.question:
B"H

In addition to the general discussion of evolution in the Torah, which is discussed elsewhere here, I was just wondering a specific detail:

How do those who propose that the Torah allows for the possibility that all organic life is descended from the same ancestor explain how the Torah prohibits two "kinds" of animals to be worked together, or how the Torah law can have anything to say about any species of animal, such as kosher laws?

Maybe a pig will evolve at a future time to resemble a cow. Is it kosher then? Seemingly not.

The fact that the Torah assigns unique roles to animals based on their "type" (same word used in Genesis when referring to how He created all "types" separate) implies that it's not possible for one "type" to evolve into another.

When one would think that the species change on their own, they can keep changing, which means the Torah's laws wouldn't be eternal.

A pig could easily continue evolving to grow more stomachs or any non kosher species could continue evolving to gain kosher signs.

But the mitzvos and commandments are eternal.

When He creates all species fully formed and individually, then those species will exist forever.

If they just happened to exist the way they do for a limited time, then the commandments of the Torah wouldn't be eternal. But we know they are (Rambam, Mishneh Torah).

On the flip side, certain animal species are required for Mitzvos, like the Paschal lamb, and need to have specific signs in order to be kosher.

What if a lamb later evolved to not have split hooves? Then not only would we not be able to eat what the Torah tells us to eat, but we wouldn't be able to ever offer the Paschal sacrifice again.

All of the daily sacrifices have to be a specific type of kosher animal. If any of those species evolved to a new one, with different features that render it not kosher, then we wouldn't be able to offer those sacrifices.

But we know that we will always be able to offer sacrifices, after moshiach comes, because the laws of the Torah are eternal.

Has there ever been any discussion of this specific point?

answers.text:
Has there ever been any discussion of this specific point?

Rabbi Dovid Brown asserts the same point as you in his work "Mysteries of the Creation". In it, he points out that all of the minim were created at ma'aseh bereshit, and it is not possible for any new minim to come into being, even though it is possible for new species within a min to diversify. Chullin 70b is proof the offspring can never be a new min from its parents.

He gives the example of the zunin, which the midrash (Bereshit Rabbah 28:8) claims diversified from wheat before the mabul, and therefore is no kilayim with wheat.

I am not saying this argument is water-tight, but it certainly seems to be the same argument you are making.

Maybe a pig will evolve at a future time to resemble a cow. Is it kosher then? Seemingly not.

It may be kosher then, Bekhorot 24a states

If one saw a young animal resembling a pig that was trailing after a ewe, the ewe is exempt from having its future offspring counted a firstborn. And the pig-like animal is forbidden for consumption “until he comes and instructs righteousness to you” (Hosea 10:12), i.e., until Elijah the prophet arrives and determines the halakha.

Rabbenu Bahye (Vayikra 11:4) writes that some interpret a Midrash (Tanhuma Buber Sh'mini, Kohelet Rabbah 1:9) that a pig will be kosher in the future. See also Recanati (Shmini), Shlah (Haye Sarah), and plenty of other Aharonim.

Obviously many (like Radvaz 2:828 and R' Bahye himself) interpret that Midrash differently.

questions.title_en: What was the Night in Genesis 1?
questions.question: A common interpretation is that the Light created on the first day in Genesis is the Wisdom of God personified in Proverbs 8. What then is the Night? And what is the significance of a "Day" in the creation (a period of light/wisdom followed by a period of darkness)? After all, it is not the sun, moon and stars by which a Day is measured in Genesis - since those are created on the fourth "day."

answers.text:
The performance of Mitzvot are the actualization of the (Will and) Wisdom of God.

Bereshit Rabbah comments on Genesis 1:5 that the night represents the deeds of the wicked, and the day represents the deeds of the righteous, and their inclusion in "one day" represents Yom Kippur, which affects atonement for the deeds of the wicked, joining them with the deeds of the righteous.

The Lubavitcher Rebbe draws from this (according to Rabbi Zaev Einhorn) that the night, being dark, represents Mitzvot that are performed without the correct intention. They do not "shine" with God's Light, as intention is a vital component of the Mitzva - the intention that it be done as actualization of God's Will, with their whole mind, heart and soul.

[... and the day represents Mitzvot performed with the correct intention, which shine with the revelation of God's Light]

questions.title_en: Shoresh Neshama
questions.question:
When we say shoresh neshama, is there a different root for each level of the soul (nefesh, ruach, neshama) or only for the level of the neshama?

For exemple, Arizal says that Nadav ben Aharon has only his ruach from the level of Kayin but his nefesh came from his elder Aminadav. So what is his shoresh neshama?

Do we have only one or several shorshei neshama?

answers.text: The Nefesh, Ruach and Neshama can all have a different shoresh. Source: Shaar Hagilgulim 1-4

questions.title_he: התחייבות בכתיבה שלא ללבוש ג'ינס - האם זה נדר?
questions.question:
שלום וברכה כבוד הרב לפני כמה חודשים אני וחברה שלי העברנו פתקים בשיעור ובאחד הפתקים רשמתי שאני לא ילבש גינס או שנראלי לא ילבש לא זוכרת את המילים המדויקות שרשמתי ואני לא בטוחה אם רשמתי בלי נדר בדרך כלל. אני מאוד משתדלת לרשום בלי נדר האם זה נקרא נדר?? אשמח לתשובה בהקדם האפשרי תודה רבה!!

שלום וברכה,
הכל בסדר, אין בזה חשש נדר.  
אמנם לפי ההלכה אדם שאומר שהוא יעשה מעשה מצווה או דבר טוב, למשל שהוא ילמד פרק משנה - הרי זה נדר (נדרים ח). וכן אם אדם נוהג שלש פעמים מעשה טוב ולא אמר שזה בלי נדר הרי שזה נחשב לנדר. מכל מקום בענייננו יש שלש סיבות שאין לחשוש לנדר:  
א. לעניין קבלה לעשות דבר טוב (בלי אמירת לשון נדר) או מנהג טוב שלש פעמים כתבו הפוסקים שניתן לסמוך על ההתרת נדרים שאנו עושים בערב ראש השנה, או לחילופין בכל נדרי שאומרים בתחילת יום כיפור, שבו אנחנו מתירים את הנדרים של השנה הקודמת וכן מכריזים במודעה שכל הנדרים שלנו להבא - אינם נדרים (הליכות שלמה ראש השנה, א, ט, דרך אמונה, שם, ציון הלכה נז).
 
ב. יש מחלוקת גדולה אם נדרים בכתב נחשבים נדרים. דעת רוב הפוסקים שאין תוקף לנדרים בכתיבה (ראה נודע ביהודה מהדו"ק יו"ד סי' סח, ובאהלה של תורה יו"ד סי' עב).
  
ג. יתכן שחצאית מג'ינס זה קצת פחות דרך צניעות, אינני יודע.
בכל מקרה לא נראה שמי שקיבלה על עצמה שלא ללבוש ג'ינס שיש להגדיר זאת כקבלה של דבר מצוה לעניין נדר. 

כל טוב!


הרחבה:
הערת הג"ר שלמה הירש שליט"א:
"לגבי א, הרבה מאוד נשים אינן עושות את המודעה בערב ר"ה ולא מתירות בבית הכנסת. גם לגבי כל נדרי יש נוסחים שמתירים רק לשעבר, ויש כאלה שבכלל לא יודעות שזה מודעה ואין דעתם לזה. הטעם האחרים שייכים. גם יתכן שלא כתבה כך בתור קבלה אלא שמספרת על כך לחברתה ואין בזה נדר".

היי אני בת 18 ורציתי לדעת מה קורה בעצם אם אני בתהליך גיור ויהיה לי בן זוג יכריחו אותנו להתחתן או שלא יגיירו אותי אבל אני צעירה ולא רואה את עצמי מתחתנת בזמן הקרוב. 
זה אומר שאסור לי בן זוג יהודי עד שאתגייר ואחרי הגיור יהיה לי מותר או שאסור לי אף פעם?

ב"ה 
שלום וברכה
אסור ליהודי לקיים יחסים עם גויה. מותר להתחתן עם גיורא רק לכהן אסור.

questions.title_he: בספירת העומר במחשבה האם ניתן להמשיך ולספור בהמשך בברכה
questions.question:
שלום לרב,
אתמול בתפילת ערבית שכחתי לספור ספירת העומר (23 ימים). 
יש לנו בבית לוח ספירת העומר עם כיתוב מלא של הספירה כפי שהיא נאמרת בדיבור. היום בצהריים ראיתי את הכרטיס הנכון  "היום עשרים ושלושה יום שהם שלושה שבועות ושני ימים לעומר", וזה הזכיר לי שלא ספרתי ושצריך לספור תכף. אני זוכר שאפילו חשבתי על החיבור של הספרות 2 ו-3 במספר הימים וגם במספר השבועות, אבל רגע אח"כ שכחתי לספור בפה.
נזכרתי בשעה 20:05 הערב (חצי שעה אחרי השקיעה), ואמרתי את הספירה של 23 בלי ברכה.
בהמשך הערב ספרתי 24 בלי ברכה.
האם אני יכול להמשיך לספור בברכה?
תודה רבה

כיון שלא הייתה ספירה בפועל, בפה, למשך כל היממה.
תמשיך לספור בלי ברכה.
תכוון לצאת בברכת החזן, או כאשר אתה מתפלל ללא מניין תבקש שיברך להוציא אותך ידי חובה.

questions.title_en: Story about the Chofetz Chaim being sworn in as a witness in a secular court
questions.question:
I remember hearing a story about the Chofetz Chaim being sworn in as a witness in a secular court. Can anyone tell me a source for this story, or give me more details? I'm 90% sure it was the Chofetz Chaim, but maybe it was some other gadol?

The story goes (as far as I can remember) that after he was sworn in, he was asked to tell about himself, so he started to list all of his accomplishments and qualifications. The Judge then said, "We heard that you were a righteous, humble person, what's with all of this boasting? The Chofetz Chaim answered, "I swore to tell the whole truth."

answers.text:
It's usually told about R' Yechezkel Abramsky. Here's Ohr Somayach's version:

When the practice of ritual slaughter was under attack in Great Britain, the famed Rabbi Yechezkel Abramsky was called to court in its defense.

The judge read from the deposition which lay before him: "Rabbi Abramsky," said the judge, "it says here that you are the foremost authority of Jewish Law in the British Empire. Is that true?" "That is true, your honor."

"And that you are the most eloquent spokesman for Jewish Law in the British Empire?"

"That is also true, your honor."

"It also says here that you are the most senior rabbi in the British Empire. Is that correct?"

"That is correct, your Honor."

Taken aback by the Rabbi's straight-forward responses, the judge said, "Rabbi Abramsky, how do you resolve your answers with the Talmudic teachings of humility?"

"It is indeed a problem, your honor," said the Rabbi. "But I'm under oath."

questions.title_en: What is the strict Torah law of tattoos?
questions.question:
I am not a rabbi, nor am I Jewish. If anything I’m a Noahide. So I want to ask strictly speaking what is the prohibition of tattoos in Torah?

From my fast study it seems that only a tattoo for idol worship, tattooing Gods Name are prohibited.

answers.text:
The Torah commands:

וְשֶׂ֣רֶט לָנֶ֗פֶשׁ לֹ֤א תִתְּנוּ֙ בִּבְשַׂרְכֶ֔ם וּכְתֹ֣בֶת קַֽעֲקַ֔ע לֹ֥א תִתְּנ֖וּ בָּכֶ֑ם אֲנִ֖י יְהוָֽה׃ You shall not make gashes in your flesh for the dead, or incise any marks on yourselves. I am the Lord. [Leviticus 19:28]

This prohibits tattoos. The Mishnah confirms it. [Makkot 3:6]. However, paint and stick-ons are allowed, but discouraged because they may appear to be tattoos – the concern is marit ayin, the appearance of a transgression.

There are no penalties for tattoos. Tattoo removal is not mandatory. Therefore, Holocaust survivors and other victims don’t have to go through the pain, risk and expense of having their tattoo removed. There are no restrictions on the burial to Jews who have tattoos, no limit on their participation in synagogue rituals, and someone with a tattoo may convert to Judaism.

questions.title_en: What do I do when I run into a gemara that is contrary to common sense
questions.question: What do I do when an answer in the Gemara seems so illogical or contrary to common sense, even after reading all the commentaries? Do I just ignore my own logic? Just saying it may make sense in the future is not sufficient.

answers.text:
Traditional commentaries generally don't deal with trying to make an argument sound logical, but rather with settling contradictions (of statements or of logic). If you are new to Gemara then the logic can be at odds with your way of thinking. But it is taken for granted that it is indeed logical. If your efforts are spent on making sense of it, rather than judging it, you will eventually be able to neatly wrap your brain around the Gemara's logic.

There are a few types of answers that might require a general introduction. For example, reading words into a Braysa or splitting statements into multiple opinions. But I doubt that you have come across this problem very often, and this wouldn't be a bad place to bring them up when you do.

Understand the Gemara the way the Rambam said to understand it:

Astrology is a disease, not a science... It is a tree under whose shadow all sorts of superstitions thrive. ... Only fools and charlatans lend value to it. [Rambam, Responsa 2:25b]

I know that you may… find sayings of… sages in the Talmud and Midrashim whose words appear to maintain that at the moment of a man's birth, the stars will cause such and such to happen to him. Do not regard this as a difficulty… Possibly the matter was hidden from them. Or there may be an allusion in those words. Or they may have been said with a view to the times and the business before them. (You surely know how many of the verses of the Torah are not to be taken literally…) [Rambam, Letter on Astrology]

questions.title_en: Guide to the Hebrew Cantillation Marks, what patterns are allowed, and how they are organized?
questions.question:
I am doing work on a Hebrew dictionary (amongst other language dictionaries), and I spent quite a bit of time working on a Hebrew transliterator to help in natural language processing (beside the point). In doing so, I ran into the ~30 or so Hebrew cantillation marks, and wanted to learn a little about them, how they work, how the writer knows where to put the marks, how the notes and rhythms get defined/allowed, and generally the theory behind how to interpret them.

The best and pretty much only example I could find on the web was this quick video, leading to learntrope.com, which at least provides a somewhat simple introduction immersion. But it doesn't still explain how they work. This video was as close as I've gotten to really understanding how to apply the principles.

The site https://mechon-mamre.org/c/hr/ has some info about Kings, Dukes, Counts, etc., and disjunctions and conjuctions, and Wikipedia has a bunch of stuff somewhat explaining their history and how they work at a very high level (not a practical level).

Wikipedia groups them, like into this 2nd-level group, and it shows the possible variations of what can occur:

The following variations of the Etnachta group can occur:

  • Mercha, Tipcha, Munach, Etnachta
  • Mercha, Tipcha, Etnachta
  • Tipcha, Munach, Etnachta
  • Tipcha, Etnachta
  • Munach, Etnachta
  • Etnachta

But why are just those variations allowed and not others? I don't follow. And how do they know "these are the variations"?

Then it shows a quick image, which I have no idea (1) how to read, or (2) how it got created (who decided on this progression of notes?):

So some questions as a beginner:

  1. What is a good way online to learn about how this works? I purchased a book on Amazon (one of the less-expensive books), and there seem to be some good $70+ books which is a little pricey. Oh also this 270 page research paper THE SYNTAX OF MASORETIC ACCENTS IN THE HEBREW BIBLE is pretty good, but it also doesn't go into how it works in practice as far as I could tell.
  2. Do any new Hebrew documents outside the 2 main books that originated the cantillation marks, get written? If so, how do the authors decide where to put the cantillation marks?
  3. Is it possible to learn without the melody/singing/chanting aspect of it, and at first just focus on the pausing and rhythms? If so, what is a recommended technique? If not, why not?

Basically, I would like to learn how this works in more detail, but didn't find anything good online to really dig into, beyond the few resources I linked.

questions.title_he: אדם שחי עם אישה אסורה-האם רשאי לעלות לתורה
questions.question:
שלום וברכה לרב, האם אדם שחי עם אישה בחטא, מה שנקרא "ידועה בציבור", ו10 מתפללים מבית הכנסת יודעים את זה עליו, שזה נחשב שנעשה בפרהסיה, האם רשאי לעלות לתורה במצב הזה, האם זאת הוכחה חותכת לכך שבוודאות עוברים על איסור נידה, או שכל עוד אין הוכחה חותכת לכך שבוודאות האישה אינה טובלת, אז זה תקין, ואז האיסור הוא רק מדרבנן ורשאי לעלות לתורה

שלום.
אם אדם בא לבית הכנסת כדי להתפלל,  מותר להעלותו לתורה.
אם מחלל שבת בפרהסיא, זה פוסל אותו מלעלות.

שלום רב,
אני מתגוררת בבית סבתי שנפטרה.
כאשר התחלנו לסדר את הבית לקראת מעבר למגורים כאן (עברתי יחד עם בן זוגי) מצאתי כאן את השיניים התותבות שלה וגם קבוצת שיער אותה גזרה ושמרה.
חששתי מהעיסוק בדברים הללו ולכן אחסנתי אותם בתא המטען של הרכב שלי, לאחר תקופה שכחתי מהם.
אבי מצא את השיניים התותבות וקבר אותן סמוך לקבר שלה.
לאחרונה מצאתי גם את שיער ראשה (אשר ככל הנראה היא גזרה ושמרה בעודה בחיים, זה ההסבר ההגיוני שסברתי לעצמי).
אני נמנעת מלספר על כך לאבי משום שאיני רוצה לגרום לו צער וכאב אך מצד שני איני רוצה להמשיך להסתובב עם שיערות ראשה באוטו שלי. 
מבחינה הלכתית, מה עליי לעשות? האם עליי לבקש מאבי שיקבור את השיער שלה או שמא יש פתרון אחר, שלא יחלל את כבוד המת ואולי גם לא אהיה חייבת לשתף אותו בנושא? 
אודה לתשובתכם ומי ייתן ותבורכו על כל עזרתכם!

שערות הנפטר שלא היו מחוברות בזמן הפטירה, כמו אצל סבתך שהיא גזרה בחייה, לא חייב בקבורה, אם לא שייך לתרום את השיער, תניחי בתוך שקית בפח.

questions.title_en: What do the field animals represent in Genesis 2?
questions.question:
Continuing my studies of Genesis, I'm curious what do the field animals represent? Man was placed in the Garden to cultivate and tend it, with the Tree of Life and the Tree of the Knowledge of Good & Evil at its center. God sets out to create a helper for Adam, and he starts by creating the field animals. Only after Adam names and evaluates all of them, and doesn't find a suitable helper, does God subsequently make Eve.

Since these are specifically animals of the field (vs animals in general) it would seem that the type of help they provide is in cultivating and tending the Garden. That is man's job and so they are to help him do it. This would seem to also explain the presence of the serpent (eating rodents/pests/etc to protect the plants and produce); at least in terms of the picture being painted.

Assuming this is allegorical / metaphorical, what do the field animals represent generally? And what does the serpent represent specifically? How do they help to cultivate and tend the Tree of Life and the Tree of Knowledge of Good & Evil in the Garden?

answers.text:
While the first human was perfect, perhaps, animals were created in the world so that humans could learn proper character traits going forward.

We find in Mishlei 30:24-28 (Artscroll translation):

There are four are among the small creatures of earth who are wise having been made wise [by the Creator]. The ants are a nation that is not strong, yet they prepare their food in the summer. Badgers are a nation that is not powerful, yet they make their abode in the rock. There is no king among the locusts, yet they all go in a single swarm. The spider seizes [its prey] with its handiwork, though it dwells in the king's palace (i.e. there's abundance of delicious food, yet it still makes a web to catch its own food).

Eruvin 100b:

Rabbi Yochanan said: Had the Torah not been given, we would have learned modesty from the cat, [aversion to] theft from the ant, chastity from the dove, and [conjugal] manners from fowl.

questions.title_en: Relationship Korach, Chukat and Balak, 3 mouths
questions.question: What is the relationship or connection, if any, between the following aspect of the three parashiyot Korach, Chukat, and Balak. Each parasha mentions one of three "mouths": the mouth of the earth (Korach), the mouth of the well (Chukat), and the mouth of Balaam's donkey (Balak)?

answers.text:
Good catch that they appear in 3 consecutive parshiot. They are all among the special exceptions to nature God created just before the end of the sixth day.

Pirkei avot:

Ten things were created on the eve of the Sabbath at twilight, and these are they: [1] the mouth of the earth, [2] the mouth of the well, [3] the mouth of the donkey, [4] the rainbow, [5] the manna, [6] the staff [of Moses], [7] the shamir, [8] the letters, [9] the writing, [10] and the tablets. And some say: also the demons, the grave of Moses, and the ram of Abraham, our father. And some say: and also tongs, made with tongs

Perhaps the additional reason is the functionality of the mouths. After the sin of the spies it appeared that Hashem cut all communication with the Jewish people. The placement of the mouths is a hint that He did not. The mouth of the Earth - punishes the wicked. The mouth of the well - provides for the righteous in this world. The mouth of a donkey - communicates with everyone and more so with Jewish people. Talmud Megilla 31a, Rabbi Yoḥanan said: Wherever you find a reference in the Bible to the might of the Holy One, Blessed be He, you also find a reference to His humility adjacent to it. Mouth of a donkey - that was a level at which Bil'am could learn his lesson.

questions.title_en: Why was the snake jealous and wanted to marry Chava?
questions.question:
As we know from midrash Bereshit Rabba 18:6 and Rashi to 3:1, the snake was the only animal that could talk, and became jealous when it saw Adam and Chava having relations in the garden. The snake wanted to marry Chava. One lady asked me a while ago: "Every animal in the Garden had a wife except for Adam prior to creation of Chava. Why did the snake additionally want to marry Chava?"

Alternatively, as a the parallel question asks, if the Snake was female and had a husband, why did it want to marry Adam? What is the meaning of this Midrash about Eve in the Garden?

One can certainly explain the story using the words of Midrash haGadol 3:1 about angel S-mael, that it was not a natural occurrence. However, the story in Bereshit does not have details of midrashim, written many years later as ethical teachings, not the documentary of what actually occurred. If the snake could really have relations with Chava, why would Adam let her be alone? Is it possible to explain the story in a way that is straight and reasonable?

answers.text:
I don't know your source for suggesting that the snake was specifically jealous of Chava, but the Gemara in Sanhedrin 59b notes expressly that its jealousy was of Adam for the following reason:

מיתיבי היה ר' יהודה בן תימא אומר אדם הראשון מיסב בגן עדן היה והיו מלאכי השרת צולין לו בשר ומסננין לו יין הציץ בו נחש וראה בכבודו ונתקנא בו התם בבשר היורד מן השמים

The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita to the assertion that eating meat was prohibited to Adam: Rabbi Yehuda ben Teima would say: Adam, the first man, would dine in the Garden of Eden, and the ministering angels would roast meat for him and strain wine for him. The snake glanced at him and saw his glory, and was jealous of him, and for that reason the snake incited him to sin and caused his banishment from the Garden. According to this, evidently Adam would eat meat. The Gemara answers: There the reference is to meat that descended from heaven, which was created by a miracle and was not the meat of animals at all. (William Davidson translation and notation)

Netziv writes on Bereshis 3:1

And the serpent was more cunning, etc.: Rashi explained in the name of Midrash Rabbah that it was jealous of them, in that it saw them copulating together and desired her. But this is a wonder! As behold, every creature only desires its species, as it is found in Tractate Bava Metzia 91b: "Its species - it is drawn after its species." And behold the serpent was not lacking its female. And if it was on account of their having intercourse before the eyes of all, the serpent also did not know shame.

Rather the matter is that it sensed that the clinging of the women to her husband was not like its female to it, which only occurred at the time of arousal for copulation. And that is only by happenstance and preparation for the thing. Which was not the case with the woman, who constantly clung to him: Given that she was the bone of his bones, the clinging was even more than a brother and sister. For they too are one flesh. However they are nevertheless not truly so like the first woman to Adam, who was like a limb to the head. And it was jealous of this.

And behold the matter is understood that the serpent never spoke. For if it had originally spoken but was cursed to be dumb and silent, why is this curse not mentioned? Moreover, speech depends on intelligence, and as per Rashi's explanation of, "and so man became a living soul" Genesis 2:7) - with speech and intelligence. And likewise did Onkelos translate, "With a speaking spirit." Behold man was unique in this virtue. However it was the constellation of the serpent that clothed himself with jealousy and spoke at that time from the throat of the serpent.

As every species from all that was created - even the botanic - has a constellation; and that is the angel that is appointed upon that species to protect it and grow it, so that it not cease from the world. And this is like the Sages, may their memory be blessed, said, "You have no [blade of] grass below without its constellation above striking it and saying to it, 'Grow!'" And the constellation of the serpent was like [the serpent]; as it was jealous of man's clinging to his Creator, may He be blessed. And it is just as we explained in the previous section, that Adam clung so greatly to God, like a portion that always yearns for its source; which is not the case with an angel. It is just separated and it is not clinging and yearning for His light, may He be blessed, except for at the time designated for song and that which is similar. And the angel was jealous about Adam; and the physical serpent about his wife. And [about] that which all of this is not explained in Scripture, the Ramban has already written, in Parashat Bechukotai - and we brought it earlier (Haamek Davar on Bereishit 1:1) - that regarding things that are not grasped by everyone, the Torah only spoke about it by hinting.

questions.question:
שלום רב, 
בעלי חילוני ואני דתיה ואנו שומרים שבת יחד, מה שדורש מבעלי ויתורים רבים ופשרות 
בעלי כבר לא נוסע בשבת, לא מבשל וכו, אך הוא עדיין צופה מדי פעם  בטלויזיה בשבת כי בשבילו זהו עונג השבת שלו. הוא מבקש פעמים רבות שאצטרף אליו אחרת הוא לא נהנה וטוען שזה פוגם לו בשמחת השבת, בייחוד לאור הוויתורים שהוא עושה עבורי.
האם זה בסדר שאשב לידו ואצפה אם איני מדליקה את הטלוויזיה? 
תודה רבה 

בס"ד
שלום לך.
ראשית ברצוני לבקש את סליחתך על העיכוב שלי בכתיבת התשובה.
מאוד מרגש לקרוא את מכתבך, על שאת שומרת מצוות למרות המציאות הלא פשוטה של לחיות עם בעל לא דתי.
אין ספק שדבר זה דורש מסירות והקרבה. ומאוד מיוחד שהוא מוכן כך להקריב ולהשקיע בזוגיות שלכם. אני מתאר לעצמי שלא קל לו בדברים שונים, והוא מגלה בכך גבורה נפשית מאוד מיוחדת.
אכן, יש פערים בין חיים של דתיים לבין חיים של אלו שלא, ולחיות בזוגיות טובה, למרות שזה ודאי אפשרי, זה מאתגר.
לכן, ממש כל הכבוד לכם שאתם שומרים על האיזון הנכון, על הבניה הנכונה וזוכים לחיות ביחד מתוך מסירות והתחשבות.
מאוד יפה שהוא עצמו התקדם בדברים כאלו חשובים, וחשוב מאוד לעודד אותו ולשבח אותו על כך.
ביחס לראיית הטלויזיה שלך. דבר זה אסור בשבת לגמרי. זה תחום שאי אפשר להתפשר בו, כי הוא נגד שמירת השבת.
כמו שלא אוכל לומר לאדם שישמור שבת ורק בדבר אחד לא ישמור שאין בכך היגיון, כך גם לשבת ולצפות בטלוויזיה זה לא שמירת שבת.
חלק מהלכות שבת זה שלא ליהנות מחילול שבת של מישהו אחר. לכן הסתכלות בטלוויזיה זה איסור של כל מי שצופה, גם אם הוא לא עושה אף מעשה. בכל הדברים האלו יש המון דברים שמחללים את השבת ולכן אסור ליהנות מכך. 
אני יודע שדבר זה מאתגר, לא קל, אבל חשוב מאוד להיות אמיתיים, שרק על ידי האמת בונים באמת.
אז מה כן לעשות?
חשוב מאוד לדעת שזוגיות זה משהו שצריך תמיד להשקיע בו. ככל שתשקיעי בו תזכי לבנות יחד עם בעלך זוגיות יותר טובה שתתרום לכם ולכל הסובבים אתכם. 
דבר זה מאוד נכון לכל זוג, ובפרט לכם, שיש לכם באופן טבעי פערים רוחניים ודתיים, שחשוב מאוד להגיע למצב שהפערים האלו לגמרי לא מפריעים בזוגיות, והזוגיות כל הזמן ניזונת מהמשותף ומהנתיתנה ההדדית.
לכן, השקיעי בדברים שמחברים ביניכם, ובפרט בחוויות המותרות ביום השבת. יש המון דברים שיכולים להיות עונג שבת, גם אם לא מחללים שבת. אם תרצי אוכל לתת לכם רעיונות שונים לכך.
חשוב לשאוף להגיע למצב שחוסר ההסתכלות בטלוויזיה  לא תפריע גם לו.
השקיעו בכך ותגלי המון הצלחה בזוגיות ובשמירת המצוות.
בברכת הצלחה רבה
הרב יצחק גרינבלט.

questions.title_en: Why does Kabbalah use the term "olamot" conjugated in the feminine when the Tanakh conjugates it as "olamim" in the masculine?
questions.question: I'm curious why "olam" would be conjugated in the feminine throughout Kabbalah (as in the "arba'ah olamot") when as far as I know it is a masculine noun and is conjugated with the "olamim" ending in Tanakh. A brief search suggests that olamim refers to worlds (space) and olamot refers to eternities (time), but I haven't found a source to explain or confirm this idea.

answers.text:
A similar case appears in the Gemara in Chullin 137b:

כי סליק איסי בר היני אשכחיה לר' יוחנן דקא מתני ליה לבריה רחלים אמר ליה אתנייה רחלות א"ל כדכתיב (בראשית לב, טו) רחלים מאתים אמר ליה לשון תורה לעצמה לשון חכמים לעצמן
§ When Isi bar Hini ascended from Babylonia to Eretz Yisrael, Rabbi Yoḥanan found him teaching the mishna to his son. Isi taught that the obligation of the first sheared wool applies only in the case of sheep [reḥelim], the masculine plural form of raḥel, meaning a sheep. Rabbi Yoḥanan said to Isi: You should teach him using the term reḥelot, the feminine plural form. Isi said to him in reply: I teach the mishna in accordance with that which is written: “Two hundred reḥelim” (Genesis 32:15). Rabbi Yoḥanan said to Isi: The language of the Torah is distinct and the language of the Sages is distinct, i.e., these are like two separate languages, and the Sages do not always use the same forms that appear in the Bible. In this case, they use reḥelot rather than reḥelim.

The commentary Ben Yehoyada says that the form that ends with ת implies more connection between the individuals than the one that doesn't (see there for why that is important in the Rabbinic context.) Perhaps the Kabbalists are trying to emphasize the connectedness of the worlds, which is a foundational principle of Chazal's worldview (see Ramchal's introduction to Aggadta.)

The word Olamim in the Bible refers to periods of time. An olam is a long time (sometimes 50 years), and olamim is many periods of time, often eternity (see here). Olamot in the Rabbinic literature refers to spiritual realms.

questions.title_en: Why mention Balak ben Tzipor?
questions.question:
In Parashat Balak 22:10 it says,

וַיֹּ֥אמֶר בִּלְעָ֖ם אֶל־הָאֱלֹהִ֑ים בָּלָ֧ק בֶּן־צִפֹּ֛ר מֶ֥לֶךְ מוֹאָ֖ב שָׁלַ֥ח אֵלָֽי׃

Balaam said to God, “Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab, sent me this message:

Many of the commentaries comment and mention why the need to say “King of Moab”, but I haven’t seen anyone mention why he had to say “son of Tzipor”. Just say Balak king of Moab. Any reason why he mentioned it?

answers.text:
In addition to my comment (I still stand by it :-)) note the approach of the Bnei Yissaschar in his Agra DeKallah who picks up on the specific mention of Tzippor minus the vav - i.e. צפר as opposed to צפור.

He wants to demonstrate that the referencing of ben Tzippor was a backwards way of acknowledging how Bilam superseded the king, as he alone had the power to bring down the Jewish people.

He writes:

וכן האזינה עדי בנו צפ"ר (במדבר כג יח). והנראה דהנה בעסק מעשה הכשפים היה בלק יותר מבלעם (במ"ר פ"כ ז'), כי בלעם היה כוחו בדיבור ובלק במעשה, ובלעם לגודל גבהות לבו רצה להראות שצריך לו מכל וכל, כי אין כח בלק גם במעשה זולתו. על כן אמר חסר ו', כבר ידעת כי ו' מורה על המעשה, וכן האזינה עדי בנו צפ"ר, אמר לו לעגמת נפש שמעשיו אינם חשובים כלום למעשה:

And refer similarly to "Give ear unto me, son of Tzippor" (Bamidbar 23:18) (i.e. also spelt without the vav) which indicates that here in the witchcraft business, Balak was greater than Bilam (see Bamidbar Rabbah 20:7) since Bilam's strength was in speech and Balak's was in action. And Bilam in his great arrogance wanted to show that he was needed more than anyone else, for there is no power of Balak even in the actions of others. Therefore, Tzippor is spelt without the vav, since you already know that vav intimates/teaches about action (and here Balak was not able to show that sense of action), likewise when he said "Give ear unto me, son of Tzippor". He told him angrily that his actions meant nothing in fact

Mabye we need to focus on pasuk 22:9, "וַיָּבֹ֥א אֱלֹהִ֖ים אֶל־בִּלְעָ֑ם וַיֹּ֕אמֶר מִ֛י הָאֲנָשִׁ֥ים הָאֵ֖לֶּה עִמָּֽךְ׃, "Hashem came to Bilam and said, “What do these men want of you?”

Rashi quoting Midrash Tanchuma Balak 5 says:

מי האנשים האלה עמך. לְהַטְעוֹתוֹ בָא, אָמַר פְּעָמִים שֶׁאֵין הַכֹּל גָּלוּי לְפָנָיו, אֵין דַּעְתּוֹ שָׁוָה עָלָיו, אַף אֲנִי אֶרְאֶה עֵת שֶׁאוּכַל לְקַלֵּל וְלֹא יָבִין (תנחומא):

"By putting this question Hashem intended to trick Bilam. And indeed Bilam thereupon said: “It seems, then, that there are times when everything is not manifest to Him; His knowledge is not always alike. I will select a time when I can curse and when He will not observe it."

As a side point, the Maskil L'David on Bamidbar 22:9 says:

מי האנשים וכו להטעותו וכו כלומר לנסותו אם יטעה לתלות חסרון בידיעתו ית׳ חלילה והוא טעה ואמר וכו׳ ומה שלא כפר לגמרי לומר שאין גלוי לפניו אלא אמר פעמים לפי שלא היה יכול לכפור לגמרי הואיל והיה נביא וידע בודאי מזה שהוא יתב׳ מגיד מראשית אחרית.

"...And what he did not completely deny by saying that it is not revealed before Him, but said sometimes, because he could not completely deny it since he was a prophet and knew for certain that Hashem reveals the end from the beginning." Meaning that its not that Bilam completely denied that Hashem knows everything, but its that sometimes he is not aware.

So based on Rashi we can say that mabye Bilam thinks that Chas Veshalom Hashem doesn't always know everything, so he doesn't know that Balak is "ben tzipor," meaning someone who uses birds for his magic speacil powers (as mentioned by the Or Hachaim on 22:2 quoting the Zohar Hakadosh 3:184b). Since Hashem is not always aware (according to what Bilam thinks), Bilam needs to tell Hashem of the speacil powers that Balak posseses, which gives importance and a claim/good reason to go and curse Bnei Yisrael. Thats why he is also very detailed in his answer, as if Hashem does not know who these people are and what is going on.

Hope this helps :)

Baruch Hashem I was directed to an answer that I believe answers the question and would like to share with the olam

The question was misleading. Instead of asking why mention Ben Tzipor the question should really be deeper and ask why mention Balak at all? Now this is not my question, it’s brought from Daat Zekenim on this verse whose quotes Bamidbar Rabbah 28:6:

וַיַּרְא בָּלָק, כֵּיוָן שֶׁבָּאוּ שְׁלוּחָיו אֵצֶל בִּלְעָם, אָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא (במדבר כב, ט): מִי הָאֲנָשִׁים, אָמַר לוֹ בִּלְעָם (במדבר כב, י): בָּלָק בֶּן צִפֹּר מֶלֶךְ מוֹאָב שָׁלַח אֵלָי, אָמַר רַבִּי אַבָּא בַּר כַּהֲנָא, זֶה אֶחָד מִשְׁלשָׁה בְּנֵי אָדָם שֶׁבְּדָקָן הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא וּמָצָא קָרוֹן שֶׁל מֵי רַגְלַיִם: קַיִן, חִזְקִיָה וּבִלְעָם. קַיִּן בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא (בראשית ד, ט): אֵי הֶבֶל אָחִיךָ, בִּקֵּשׁ לְהַטְעוֹת כִּבְיָכוֹל, הָיָה צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר רִבּוֹנוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם הַנִּסְתָּרוֹת וְהַנִּגְלוֹת לְפָנֶיךָ גְּלוּיוֹת, וְאַתָּה שׁוֹאֲלֵנִי בִּשְׁבִיל אָחִי, אֶלָּא אָמַר לוֹ (בראשית ד, ט): לֹא יָדַעְתִּי הַשֹּׁמֵר אָחִי אָנֹכִי, אָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא חַיֶּיךָ כָּךְ דִּבַּרְתָּ (בראשית ד, י): קוֹל דְּמֵי אָחִיךָ צֹעֲקִים. חִזְקִיָּה כְּשֶׁעָמַד מֵחָלְיוֹ שָׁלַח לוֹ מְרֹדַךְ בַּלְאֲדָן דּוֹרוֹן, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (ישעיה לט, א): בָּעֵת הַהִיא שָׁלַח מְרֹדַךְ בַּלְאֲדָן בָּא יְשַׁעְיָה אָמַר לוֹ (ישעיה לט, ג): מָה אָמְרוּ הָאֲנָשִׁים הָאֵלֶּה וּמֵאַיִן יָבֹאוּ אֵלֶיךָ, הָיָה צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר אַתְּ נָבִיא שֶׁל מָקוֹם וְלִי אַתְּ שׁוֹאֵל, אֶלָּא הִתְחִיל מִתְגָּאֶה וְאָמַר (ישעיה לט, ג): מֵאֶרֶץ רְחוֹקָה בָּאוּ אֵלַי מִבָּבֶל, אָמַר לוֹ יְשַׁעְיָה הוֹאִיל וְכָךְ אָמַרְתָּ (ישעיה לט, ו ז): הִנֵּה יָמִים בָּאִים וְנִשָֹּׂא [את] כָּל אֲשֶׁר בְּבֵיתֶךָ, וּמִבָּנֶיךָ אֲשֶׁר יֵצְאוּ מִמְךָ, וְהָיוּ סָרִיסִים בְּהֵיכַל מֶלֶךְ בָּבֶל. וְכֵן בִּלְעָם הָרָשָׁע בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁשָּׁלַח בָּלָק אֶצְלוֹ, אָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא: מִי הָאֲנָשִׁים הָאֵלֶּה עִמָּךְ, הָיָה צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר רִבּוֹנוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם הַכֹּל גָּלוּי לְפָנֶיךָ וְאֵין כָּל דָּבָר נֶעֱלָם מִמֶּךָּ וְלִי אַתְּ שׁוֹאֵל, אֶלָּא אָמַר לוֹ: בָּלָק בֶּן צִפֹּר מֶלֶךְ מוֹאָב שָׁלַח אֵלָי. אָמַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא הוֹאִיל וְכָךְ אַתָּה מְדַבֵּר (במדבר כב, יב): לֹא תָאֹר אֶת הָעָם. אָמַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא רָשָׁע שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם, כְּתִיב עַל יִשְׂרָאֵל (זכריה ב, יב): כִּי הַנֹּגֵעַ בָּכֶם כְּנֹגֵעַ בְּבָבַת עֵינוֹ, וְאַתָּה הוֹלֵךְ לִגַּע בָּהֶם וּלְקַלְּלָם, תֵּצֵא עֵינוֹ, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (במדבר כד, ג): שְׂתֻם הָעָיִן, לְקַיֵּם כָּל הַנֹּגֵעַ בָּהֶם כְּנֹגֵעַ בְּבָבַת עֵינוֹ.

“Balak…saw” – when his emissaries came to Bilam, the Holy One blessed be He said to him: “Who are [these] men…?” (Numbers 22:9). Bilam said to Him: “Balak son of Tzipor, king of Moav, sent to me” (Numbers 22:10). Rabbi Abba bar Kahana said: This is one of three people whom the Holy One blessed be He examined but found them to be a jug of urine. They are Cain, Hezekiah, and Bilam. Cain, when the Holy One blessed be He said to him: ‘Where is your brother Abel?’ he sought, as it were, to mislead. He should have said: ‘Master of the universe, the concealed and the revealed are revealed before You, and You are asking me regarding my brother?’ Instead, he said to Him: “I do not know; am I my brother’s keeper?” (Genesis 4:9). The Holy One blessed be He said to him: ‘This is how you speak? “The voice of your brother's blood cries out to Me from the ground. [Now, you are cursed…]”’ (Genesis 4:10–11). Hezekiah, when he recovered from his illness, Merodakh Baladan sent him a gift, as it is stated: “At that time, Merodakh Baladan…sent [scrolls and a gift to Hezekiah]” (Isaiah 39:1). Isaiah came and said to him: “What did those men say, and from where did they come to you?” (Isaiah 39:3). He [Hezekiah] should have said to him: ‘You are a prophet of the Omnipresent, and you are asking me?’ Instead, he began boasting: “They came to me from a distant land, from Babylonia” (Isaiah 39:3). Isaiah said to him: ‘Since that is what you said: “Behold, days are coming and everything that is in your house…will be carried [to Babylonia]…From your sons, who will descend from you…they will be officials in the palace of the king of Babylon”’ (Isaiah 39:6–7). Likewise, the wicked Bilam, when Balak sent to him, the Holy One blessed be He said to him: “Who are these men with you?” (Numbers 22:9), he should have said: ‘Master of the universe, everything is revealed before You and nothing is obscured from You, and You are asking me?’ Instead he said to him: “Balak son of Tzipor, king of Moav, sent to me.” The Holy One blessed be He said to him: ‘Since that is how you speak, “do not curse the people” (Numbers 22:12). The Holy One blessed be He said: ‘Wicked one of the world, it is written in Israel’s regard: “For one who touches you, touches the pupil of his eye” (Zechariah 2:12), and you go to accost them and curse them? Let his eye be removed, as it is stated: “One with an open eye” (Numbers 24:3), to realize: “For one who touches you, touches the pupil of his eye.”’

From here was can see that Bilam having mentioned anything to Hashem was a mistake and was “the reason” why Hashem didn’t let him curse the Jewish people. So now that we know that he didn’t mention Balak Ben Tzipor as part of a claim (as he did when he mentions “King of Moab” as Aderet Eliyahu explains that it was his hava mina that Hashem would accept his claim, if not he would not have asked), we need to understand why mention it at all? So really you can ask the same question on Cain and Adam Harishon and Chizkiyahu and say that they made a mistake and didn’t answer Hashem properly. But in this specific case we are given a glimpse of answer by taking what @Avishai Tebeka has answered and fitting it into this explanation as follows:

Bilam was a prophet and understood the greatness and power of Hashem. But as Rashi quoting Midrash Tanchuma Balak 5 says:

מי האנשים האלה עמך. לְהַטְעוֹתוֹ בָא, אָמַר פְּעָמִים שֶׁאֵין הַכֹּל גָּלוּי לְפָנָיו, אֵין דַּעְתּוֹ שָׁוָה עָלָיו, אַף אֲנִי אֶרְאֶה עֵת שֶׁאוּכַל לְקַלֵּל וְלֹא יָבִין (תנחומא):

Bilam clearly mistakenly believed that there are times where Hashem, Chas veShalom, isn’t aware/doesn’t know and can be taken advantage of. Now in the context of this explanation it is difficult to understand how Bilam used this as a reason to ask Hashem to curse because if he truly believed that there are these times where he can curse without Hashem knowing then why even bring it up to Hashem? Just curse at this moment?! So leaving that aside we can use this to answer our question by saying that Bilam answered Hashem in this way because he believed that sometimes Hashem is not aware and when he was asked “Who are these people” he gave Hashem a genuine answer, and that was exactly his mistake. He should have understood that it’s a rhetorical question because Hashem knows everything. So he answered Hashem Balak Ben Tzipor because he thought that there are times when Hashem does not know certain things and since Hashem asked him this question he wanted to answer accordingly (he didn’t have a hava mina that it’s a rhetorical question because he didn’t believe that Hashem is always all knowing). And he mentioned King of Moab either for this same reason, or more fittingly, as a claim to be able to even ask Hashem to curse the Jewish nation as Aderet Eliyahu explains in his comment

With this we can understand not only why Bilam mentioned Ben Tzipor, but further why he mentioned Balak at all and by looking at Aderet Eliyahu also understanding why he mentioned King of Moab

questions.title_en: Source of Daat Zkenim - Parashat Balak
questions.question:
In Parashat Balak 22:10 the verse says,

וַיֹּ֥אמֶר בִּלְעָ֖ם אֶל־הָאֱלֹהִ֑ים בָּלָ֧ק בֶּן־צִפֹּ֛ר מֶ֥לֶךְ מוֹאָ֖ב שָׁלַ֥ח אֵלָֽי׃

Balaam said to God, “Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab, sent me this message:

On this verse the Daat Zkenim says that this is one of three places where a person did not respond properly to Hashem (Kayin and Chizkiyahu being the others - and he notes that really Adam harishon should also be in the list instead of Chizkiyahu…)

What is the original source that mentions that there were three people who did not respond properly to Hashem?

Thanks

answers.text:
Bamidbar Rabbah 20:6:

Rabbi Abba bar Kahana said: This is one of three people whom the Holy One blessed be He examined but found them to be a jug of urine. They are Cain, Hezekiah, and Bilam...

questions.title_en: Pronunciation based on grammatical concepts
questions.question:
There is a grammatical concept as follows, if I'm not mistaken:

If [Aleph, Hei, Yud, Vav] comes at the end of one word, the dot of the first letter in the following word is dropped.

My question is, how does this affect the pronunciation of the second word?

For example:

  1. Pirkei Avot, perek Dalet, paragraph Chaf:
    Is כְתוּבָה pronounced ketuva or chetuva?

  2. Pirkei Avot, perek Hei, paragraph Chet (last word):
    Is כַהֲלָכָה pronounced kahalacha or chahalacha?

I could be very wrong, as I’m still learning. Please correct me if so.

answers.text:
If one of the six begedkefet letters is written without a dagesh (dot inside the letter), then it is always pronounced as a fricative, rather than as a plosive.

So, in the examples you gave, the kaf appears without a dagesh and is therefore pronounced as a voiceless uvular fricative or voiceless velar fricative (depending on one's tradition) - often transliterated as 'kh' or 'ch'.

In the specific cases you mention, the Od Yosef Hai siddur (who is very exacting on this) has them both as khaf or chaf (not kaf).

The full rule you are referring to is brought in Em Lamikra Velamasoret (by Rabbi Nissan Sharoni) perek 15. It discusses beged kefet losing its daghesh when coming after an open syllable at the end of the previous word.

He brings there 5 exceptions to this rule:

  • Mapik (pronounced): if the ending letters are a Nach nireh (already implied in the way I worded the original rule).
  • Mafsik (stopped): if there is a ta'am mafsik on the word before the beged kefet, rendering the two words separate.
  • Dahik (pressed): when the previous word ends with a silent he after a patach, seghol, or kamatz, or if the word ends with a he, khaf, or thaf with a kamatz on them, and there is a makaf between that word and the beged kefet word (I believe there are exceptions to this).
  • Atei Merahik (coming from afar): when the previous word is mileil and ends with a he preceded by a seghol or kamatz, or ends with a he, khaf, or thaf with a kamatz, and the beged kefet word has its hat'amah on the first tenuah (slightly different than syllable).
  • Otiot domot (similar letters): the beged kefet word starts with two of the same letter, the first being a prefix.

None of these exceptions occur in the case listed by the OP, as they would be applied in a Mishna. So the letter כ loses the daghesh in both cases.

questions.title_en: Why is There a Switch in Grammar in Sh'ma?
questions.question:
The Sh'ma begins with Dvarim 6:4:

:שְׁמַ֖ע יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל ה׳ אֱלֹהֵ֖ינוּ ה׳ | אֶחָֽד

Hear, O Israel: The Lord is our God; the Lord is one.

Moshe speaks to the nation in the imperative/command form - "Hear"! This form is used to issue a command in the second person — that is, the command is directed at the person being spoken to.

But then the next verse immediately switches grammatical form:

וְאָ֣הַבְתָּ֔ אֵ֖ת ה׳ אֱלֹהֶ֑יךָ בְּכָל־לְבָֽבְךָ֥ וּבְכָל־נַפְשְׁך וּבְכָל־מְאֹדֶֽךָ:

And you shall love the Lord, your God, with all your heart and with all your soul, and with all your means.

Moshe now tells the nation to love God, but it is in the sequential perfect form. The sequential perfect form, true to its name, discusses a sequence of events. Here it can carry the same meaning as the verb before it - command form. Such as in לֵ֤ךְ וְאָֽמַרְתָּ֙ אֶל־עַבְדִּ֣י אֶל־דָּוִ֔ד/Go and say to my servant David (Samuel 2 7:5). And so is this a normal example of Hebrew Grammar (שמע and ואהבת are both commands) or is something else going on here?

Is the fact that the verses discuss different mitzvot - the Mitzva of God's Oneness v. the Mitzva of loving God - a clue?

answers.text:
Yes I believe your suggestion is correct - the switch in grammar has to do with the context of each statement. Let’s break it down:

The first statement that Hashem is our Gd and He is one is stated as a fact. No room to argue or to need to comprehend anything, it just is

Whereas the next verse which commands us to love Gd, even though it’s a commandment and we must do it, you cannot force someone to love something unless they do. Therefore the statement could not have been in the command form because it is something which requires each individual to think about and contemplate to reach this level of love. It’s not something black and white like knowing that Gd is one and can therefore be commanded. This is about emotions and therefore must come from a place of self desire and cannot be commanded upon.

My proof from this comes from Sefer Hamitzvot positive commandments 1, 2 and 3. It is evident from his wording that knowing that Gd exists and that He is one is just a fact that was commanded to us without room for us to think and comprehend. Whereas loving Gd he mentions how we need to contemplate and bring ourselves to understanding etc proving that it’s not something that can be commanded and therefore explains the change in grammar in the verse

According to Sefer haChinuch mitzvah 420, the first passuk is acceptance of kingship for the entire Jewish nation, while the rest of the verses speak of other important individual mitzvos listed elsewhere in the Sefer. There are also different halachic requirements to the 1st verse (Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim, 61:5-7, Ram"a and Mishna Berura there. For example, one cannot walk when reciting the first verse as a result.

questions.title_en: Shaking the Arava on Hoshana Rabbah
questions.question:
I see in S.O. O Ch 564 (4) in the Rema that it is a custom not only to beat the Arava but also to shake it.

וי"א שצריך לנענע בה [טור בשם רש"י] ונהגו לעשות שתיהן מנענעין בה ואח"כ חובטין אותה:

questions.title_he: חיבורי מוהראש הרב אליעזר שלמה שיק
questions.question:
שלום וברכה,
ברשותי ספר ״אשר בנחל״ שהעבירו לי. 
לאחר עיון קצר של אחד מבני ביתי הבנו שיש איזו בעיה סביב התוכן והמחבר. וברצוננו להוציא את הספר מהבית.
שאלתי היא האם צריך לשים את הספר בגניזה? או שצריך לזרוק אותו ממש? מה כדאי לעשות? 

תודה מראש!

שלום רב לשואלת הנכבדת.
חס ושלום מדובר על גאון וצדיק קדוש ששימש את גדולי הדור הקודם וזכה לחבר מאות ספרים ופירושים על כל התורה בנגלה ובנסתר ע"פ רבי נחמן ותלמידו הגדול רבי נתן מברסלב זי"ע. סמכו עליו והעריצו אותו באהבה יתרה גדולי הדור הקודם והוא אף זכה להחזיר רבבות יהודים בתשובה.

חושבני שהחוסר הבנה שלכם ממה שהוא כתב בשו"ת אשר בנחל נובע מכך שהוא כתב עשרות אלפי תשובות פרטניות לשאלות מכל העולם ולעיתים הוא השתמש בהדרכות שאינם שגרתיות לספרי שו"ת וגם השפה ודרך הכתיבה יכולים במבט חיצוני כאשר מתבוננים על תשובה אחת בלי מבט מקיף על תורתו הגדולה לבלבל אך ודאי שתורת אמת בפיהו.

בברכת התורה ולומדיה,

questions.title_en: Bowing during Shmonei Esrei - why only sometimes
questions.question: Why don’t we bow every time we say “Barach Ata” during Shmonei Esrei? Are you allowed to if you wanted to? Is there a specific reason why we only bow at specific brachas? Thanks

answers.text: It is a subject of Shulchan Aruch Orach Chaim 113:1 and Mishna Berurah there. Technically, one can bow at the end of each blessing and in the middle. At the beginning of a blessings it is inappropriate. The reason, so that not to uproot takanat chachamim which will make it appear that each and every praying person is stringent in accordance with his liking, and suspect to being arrogant, who want to show they are stricter than the rest of the tzibur.

questions.title_en: Instant noodles on Shabbat
questions.question:
There is a concept of Kli Sheini (a second cup) in which Halacha dictates that by taking boiling water from its source into an empty vessel and then pouring it into another vessel, the water is no longer considered to have the status of boiling as it can no longer “cook”. From my understanding that is why you’re allowed to make tea or coffee on Shabbat by using Kli Sheini.

My question is, items like instant noodles or instant couscous, which will “cook” even after Kli Sheini, would that be allowed and therefore you could cook on Shabbat, or perhaps for other reasons it would not be allowed?

האם יש תוקף הלכתי מסורתי כלשהו למעמד הזוג וביחוד האשה בחתונה רפורמית?

ב"ה 
שלום וברכה 
כאשר העדים לא כשרים - הקידושין לא חלו.

יש לי כרטיסים לטיסה חזור לישראל ב13.8 (תשעה באב) בשעה 18:00 בערב האם מותר לטוס? 

מותר לטוס בתשעה באב,
